plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two panels, (a) and (b), tracking ten fractional values through a bucket sort. Panel (a) is a vertical column of ten gray cells headed by the italic letter A, with row indices 1 through 10 running down its left side; from top to bottom the cells hold .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, and .68. Panel (b) is a second vertical column of ten gray cells headed B and indexed 0 through 9, each cell serving as the head of a linked list. The cells at indices 0, 4, 5, and 8 contain only a diagonal slash. The rest carry a horizontal arrow into a chain of two-field records, each record showing a value on the left and either a pointer arrow or a terminating slash on the right: index 1 leads to .12 then .17, index 2 to .21, .23, then .26, index 3 to .39 alone, index 6 to .68, index 7 to .72 then .78, and index 9 to .94. Each chain is in increasing order, and the leading digit of every value matches the index of the cell whose chain holds it, which is the correspondence the two columns invite the reader to check. The panels walk through distributing numbers drawn from the half-open interval from 0 to 1 into equal-width buckets, after which concatenating the sorted lists in index order gives the sorted output.

interactionPlan.concept: Bucket sort distributes uniformly distributed inputs into an array of buckets using an arithmetic mapping, preserving order so that each bucket only requires a small local sort.

interactions.teaches: The arithmetic floor(10*x) sends each value to its correct bucket. Replaying shows sequential insertions maintaining local sorted order. Changing inputs to 0.01 or 0.99 proves the half-open interval boundary conditions work without out-of-bounds errors.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Bucket sort exploits the uniform distribution of inputs by using a direct arithmetic mapping (floor(10*x)) to distribute items into small, manageable, pre-sorted buckets.

Linked list nodes should visually look like two-field records: [ value | pointer ]. The pointer field contains an arrow head originating from its center to the next node, or a diagonal slash if it's the tail. Left-align indices for both arrays. Ensure leading zeroes are omitted in the decimals (.78, not 0.78) exactly as in the original.

authoredContext:
Bucket sort assumes that the input is drawn from a uniform distribution and has an average-case running time of O.n/. Like counting sort, bucket sort is fast because it assumes something about the input. Whereas counting sort assumes that the input consists of integers in a small range, bucket sort assumes that the input is generated by a random process that distributes elements uniformly and independently over the interval Œ0; 1/. (See Section C.2 for a definition of uniform distribution.) Bucket sort divides the interval Œ0; 1/ into n equal-sized subintervals, or buckets, and then distributes the n input numbers into the buckets. Since the inputs are uniformly and independently distributed over Œ0; 1/, we do not expect many numbers to fall into each bucket. To produce the output, we simply sort the numbers in each bucket and then go through the buckets in order, listing the elements in each. Figure 8.4 shows the operation of bucket sort on an input array of 10 numbers.
